catalog_quote: In isolation, all ‘full’ words in Pangasinan, as well as many grammatical markers, have at least one strongly stressed syllable (in most cases, only one). The remaining syllables may be either moderately or weakly stressed, depending on the interplay of a number of factors ... Firstly, syllables which end in a final consonant automatically attract a moderate stress ... so that the difference between the strongly stressed syllable and its neighbor in a word like nátàn ‘now’ is less noticeable than in a word like bása ‘read’. Secondly, there is a tendency for every alternate syllable preceding or following a strongly stressed syllable to attract medium stress ... Certain affixes complicate the picture by either attracting or repelling strong stress in contiguous syllables. ... sweep_summary: Pangasinan (pang1290) is in the catalog as LEXICAL on Benton 1971 (Pangasinan Reference Grammar, pp. 24-26). The sweep had one stress-title item, Zorc 1979 'On the development of contrastive word accent: Pangasinan, a case in point' (Pacific Linguistics C-45: 241-258), already listed in the per-language bibliography and already on file at (open via DOI 10.15144/PL-C45.241 -> sealang.net, CC BY-SA). Read in full: it is a historical-comparative argument that Proto-Philippine penult length was lost in pre-Pangasinan and that modern Pangasinan re-developed contrastive penult and antepenult vowel length secondarily (compensatory lengthening from *qC and geminate clusters, borrowing, innovation), with a synchronic statement (p. 248, n. 2 p. 254) that modern Pangasinan has contrastive length (la:ga/laga, qanak/qa:nak, ka:ruman) and that stress is secondary to length (long vowel stressed; short penult -> ultima stress; stress shifts with intonation). Verdict: refines the catalog coding - confirms LEXICAL, adds that the contrast is phonemic vowel length (catalog length_phonemic currently null) and that antepenult accent occurs; does not supersede Benton 1971 as the deciding source. written in the working files. Nothing left unread; no acquisition priorities.

new_statements.quote: [p. 248] Although the original PPH length was lost in pre-Png, modern Png clearly has penult and antepenult length: la:ga 'to blanch' (#66) as opposed to laga 'to braid' (#10); qanak 'child' (#16), but qa:nak 'children' (4.2. below); ka:ruman 'yesterday' (#70). [n. 2, p. 254] Stress, taken as a primary feature of accent in Zorc (1972), is here treated as secondary to vowel length or shortness. Long vowels are generally stressed; a short penult vowel is followed by stress on the ultima (as indicated in the phonetic transcriptions given). However, stress is a syntactic feature and may shift in various sentence intonations. Vowel length is a primary feature, and is not lost.

new_statements.locator: p. 248 section 4 (first sentence) and p. 254 note 2
new_statements.reading: Modern Pangasinan word accent is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs la:ga vs laga; qanak vs qa:nak), with the contrast carried by vowel length on the penult or antepenult; stress is treated as secondary and predictable from length (long vowel stressed; short penult -> ultima stress) and may shift under sentence intonation. This confirms the catalog's LEXICAL coding (agrees with Benton 1971's láki/lakí, anák/ának pairs) and refines it: the underlying contrast is analysed as phonemic vowel length (the catalog's length_phonemic field is currently null), antepenult accent exists (ka:ruman 'yesterday', ta:wag-an), and man-/-an affixes fix length position, matching the catalog's morphology note. Zorc's paper is historical and its synchronic statement is a footnote, so it does not replace Benton's reference grammar as the deciding source.

sources.note: Historical-comparative paper: Proto-Philippine contrastive accent (penult length) was lost in pre-Pangasinan (basic-vocabulary cognates show short penults where PPH had length, e.g. dila 'tongue', kutu 'louse'; of 165 Swadesh forms in Benton 1971b only 27 have penult length, all explicable as secondary), and modern Pangasinan then redeveloped contrastive length secondarily by compensatory lengthening (loss of *qC and of the first member of geminate clusters), by borrowing, and by innovation. sources.quote: p. 12: 'the favored rhythm of speech in Pangasinan is an even alternation between stressed and unstressed syllables, with an extra heavy stress falling at the end of a sentence. In fairly rapid speech, this may result in the stressing of normally unstressed syllables in some words, and the corresponding removal of stress from syllables where it would otherwise be expected to fall.' p. 621: 'Most Pangasinan words have one strongly stressed syllable ...'; stress is marked lexically with an acute throughout the lessons ('A more detailed account is found in the reference grammar', p. 7).
